description:
Bickleigh Castle sits on the banks of the River Exe near Tiverton in Devon, and its documented history reaches back further than almost any other property in this entire pilot collection. The site's oldest structure, the Saxon Moot House — the meeting hall of an Anglo-Saxon community, today preserved as the castle's Chapel — dates to around 600 AD, centuries before the Norman Conquest reshaped English landholding and fortification. The Normans added a motte-and-bailey castle on the same ground in 1018, built specifically to defend the Bickleigh community, and the resulting complex was subsequently altered in both the 15th and 17th centuries as successive owners adapted the buildings to changing needs and tastes.

Bickleigh developed into one of Devon's most historically significant medieval manor houses, serving as the seat first of a cadet branch of the Earls of Devon and later of the Carew family, one of the county's leading gentry families. The Carews' tenure placed Bickleigh firmly on the Royalist side during the English Civil War, and the castle's most evocative historical moment came in 1644, when Queen Henrietta Maria, wife of King Charles I, stayed at Bickleigh as a guest of Sir Henry and Lady Dorothy Carew — a direct royal visit during one of the most turbulent periods in English constitutional history.

That Royalist association came at a cost. In late 1645, Bickleigh was besieged by Parliamentary forces under General Fairfax, one of the New Model Army's most effective commanders, and following the siege the castle was deliberately 'slighted' — partially demolished — to prevent it from being used for military purposes again. This practice of slighting captured Royalist strongholds was common across England during and after the Civil War, and Bickleigh's altered later form reflects this deliberate wartime damage layered onto centuries of earlier peaceful development.

Today Bickleigh operates as a 15-room bed and breakfast, its guest accommodation arranged in thatched cottages surrounding the castle's own courtyard — a genuinely distinctive architectural arrangement compared to the single large building found at most comparable properties. What sets Bickleigh apart most clearly within this collection, however, is its approach to day-visitor access: rather than relying on hotel restaurant dining, Bickleigh opens the castle, its Saxon chapel and its gardens to genuine day visitors on Thursdays, from April through October, between noon and 5pm — a real, independently structured visitor product comparable in spirit to Appleby Castle's Norman Centre in this same collection.

Visitors on these Thursday openings can choose a simple garden walk for £4 per adult, or a combined garden walk and guided tour led by the castle's resident historian for £9 per adult and £5 per child, with the guided tour departing at 2:30pm. Cream teas are served between noon and 2pm, rounding out a genuinely full afternoon's visit built around real historical content rather than a hotel amenity dressed up as an attraction. The Saxon chapel and the castle's ground floor are wheelchair accessible, a detail worth knowing given how many buildings of this age present genuine accessibility barriers. For visitors exploring Devon's Exe valley, Bickleigh offers a rare combination in this collection: over 1,400 years of continuous documented history on a single site, a real siege story, a royal guest, and a clearly priced, seasonal day-visit product built around genuine historical interpretation.

The surrounding Exe valley is itself a genuine draw beyond the castle walls, with the river offering opportunities for wild swimming and paddling on quieter stretches near Bickleigh, and the wider Mid Devon countryside providing a genuinely rural, unhurried counterpoint to Devon's better-known coastal resorts further south. Bickleigh's position within easy reach of both Exeter and Tiverton makes it a workable day-trip destination for visitors based in either town, while its limited Thursday-only opening schedule rewards those who plan their visit specifically around the castle's own calendar rather than assuming year-round or daily access.

faqs.question: Can I visit Bickleigh Castle as a day visitor?
faqs.answer: Yes, on a specific schedule: the castle, Saxon chapel and gardens are open to day visitors on Thursdays only, from April through October, between noon and 5pm. A simple garden walk costs £4 per adult, while a combined garden walk and guided tour with the resident historian, departing at 2:30pm, costs £9 per adult and £5 per child. Cream teas are served between noon and 2pm.

faqs.question: What is the oldest part of Bickleigh Castle?
faqs.answer: The oldest structure is the Saxon Moot House, today preserved as the castle's Chapel, dating to around 600 AD — centuries before the Norman motte-and-bailey castle was added to the site in 1018. This makes Bickleigh's documented history among the longest of any property in this entire collection.

faqs.question: What happened to Bickleigh Castle during the Civil War?
faqs.answer: Bickleigh was a Royalist stronghold, and Queen Henrietta Maria stayed there as a guest of Sir Henry and Lady Dorothy Carew in 1644. In late 1645, Parliamentary forces under General Fairfax besieged the castle, and afterward it was deliberately 'slighted' — partially demolished — to prevent it from being used militarily again, a common fate for captured Royalist strongholds during this period.
